docs.title: Odoo Code Snippets & Cookbook 🍳
docs.text:
Odoo 18.0 Odoo 19.0 Odoo 20.0 Ready

Welcome to the unofficial Odoo Cookbook! This repository was created to help developers and technical consultants find the correct syntax for common operations without having to dig through Odoo's source code for hours.

All snippets are ready to copy-paste, focus on modern Odoo versions, and follow the Odoo Community Association (OCA) best practices.

docs.title: How to use this Cookbook
docs.text:
Navigate through the sections using the top menu or the sidebar. The repository is structured by architectural layers to help you quickly find what you need:

  • 1. ORM & Models: Computed fields, constraints, CRUD overrides, and recordset operations.
  • 2. Views & UI (XML): Safe form inheritance, dynamic lists, search filters, and Kanban boards.
  • 3. Chatter & Mail: Activity tracking, silent logging, and dispatching template-based emails.
  • 4. Wizards: Transient models for mass updates and step-by-step modal interactions.
  • 5. Actions & Cron: Scheduled background jobs, server actions, and automated triggers.
  • 6. OWL & Frontend: Modern JavaScript UI, custom field widgets, and component patching (hooks & lifecycle).
  • 7. Migration & Versions: Quick reference guides for upgrading code syntax to Odoo 18, 19, and 20.
  • 8. Best Practices & Pitfalls: Common mistakes (N+1 queries, Expected Singleton, Context pollution) and how to write clean, optimized code.

!!! tip "Contribute" Do you have a brilliant snippet you use in every project? Open a Pull Request on the GitHub repository to add it!

docs.title: ORM & Models
docs.text: A comprehensive reference for working with the Odoo Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) layer, business logic hooks, validations, and transient interactions.

docs.title: 1. Computed Fields (@api.depends)
docs.text:
Computed fields calculate their values on the fly or persist them using store=True. Always decorate compute methods with @api.depends so Odoo knows when to recalculate them.

from odoo import models, fields, api

class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'

    total_weight = fields.Float(
        string='Total Weight (kg)',
        compute='_compute_total_weight',
        store=True,  # Set to True to allow sorting and filtering in list/search views
        help="Aggregated weight of all order lines."
    )

    @api.depends('order_line.product_id.weight', 'order_line.product_uom_qty')
    def _compute_total_weight(self):
        for order in self:
            weight = 0.0
            for line in order.order_line:
                weight += (line.product_id.weight or 0.0) * line.product_uom_qty
            order.total_weight = weight

!!! tip "Inverse & Search on Compute Fields" If you need users to manually edit a computed field, define an inverse='_inverse_method'. If store=False and you need to filter on it, define a search='_search_method'.

docs.title: 2. Business Validation Constraints (@api.constrains)
docs.text:
Use @api.constrains for complex cross-field validations that cannot be handled by simple database constraints (_sql_constraints).

from odoo import models, fields, api
from odoo.exceptions import ValidationError

class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'

    expected_delivery = fields.Date(string="Expected Delivery Date")

    @api.constrains('expected_delivery', 'date_order')
    def _check_expected_delivery(self):
        for record in self:
            if record.expected_delivery and record.date_order:
                if record.expected_delivery < record.date_order.date():
                    raise ValidationError(
                        "The expected delivery date cannot precede the order confirmation date."
                    )

docs.title: 3. Overriding CRUD Methods (create & write)
docs.text:
When intercepting record creation, always implement @api.model_create_multi to support batch imports and high-performance multi-record creation.

from odoo import models, fields, api

class CustomTask(models.Model):
    _name = 'custom.task'
    _description = 'Custom Task with Sequence'

    name = fields.Char(
        string='Reference',
        required=True,
        copy=False,
        readonly=True,
        default='New'
    )
    is_urgent = fields.Boolean(default=False)

    @api.model_create_multi
    def create(self, vals_list):
        for vals in vals_list:
            if vals.get('name', 'New') == 'New':
                # Fetch reference from ir.sequence
                vals['name'] = (
                    self.env['ir.sequence'].next_by_code('custom.task.code') or 'New'
                )
        return super().create(vals_list)

    def write(self, vals):
        # Example: pre-write hook
        if 'is_urgent' in vals and vals['is_urgent']:
            # Perform custom pre-update validation or side effects
            pass
        return super().write(vals)

docs.title: 4. Recordset Operations (filtered, mapped, sorted)
docs.text:
Avoid running nested Python loops over database records. Use Odoo's native recordset utilities to maintain fast, readable, in-memory operations.

# 1. Search with standard domain
confirmed_orders = self.env['sale.order'].search([
    ('state', '=', 'sale'),
    ('partner_id.country_id.code', '=', 'IT'),
])

# 2. Filter records in memory using a lambda or field name
high_value_orders = confirmed_orders.filtered(lambda order: order.amount_total >= 5000)

# 3. Extract attributes or linked records into lists / recordsets
customer_emails = confirmed_orders.mapped('partner_id.email')  # Python list of unique emails
all_order_lines = confirmed_orders.mapped('order_line')         # Flat recordset of sale.order.line

# 4. Sort recordsets in memory
sorted_orders = confirmed_orders.sorted(key=lambda o: o.date_order, reverse=True)

docs.title: 5. Modifying Environment & Context (with_context)
docs.text:
The context carries session metadata (active language, default values, user timezone). You can pass keys to alter behavior or silence background jobs during heavy batch operations.

# Silence chatter notifications and tracking during bulk migrations
bulk_orders = self.env['sale.order'].browse([10, 11, 12])

bulk_orders.with_context(
    tracking_disable=True,
    mail_auto_subscribe_no_notify=True,
    mail_create_nolog=True
).write({'state': 'done'})

# Read translated field values in a specific language
french_name = self.env['product.product'].with_context(lang='fr_FR').browse(1).name

docs.title: Views & UI (XML)
docs.text: Extending and customizing Odoo views is one of the most common tasks in module development. Odoo uses an XML-based inheritance engine that resolves view trees in memory during load time without modifying upstream source code.

docs.title: 1. XPath Inheritance Rules & Target Positions
docs.text:
When targeting nodes in existing views, prioritize stable technical identifiers (like name="...") over volatile CSS classes or arbitrary tag positions.

Position Effect Best For after Inserts sibling node immediately following the match Adding companion fields or buttons before Inserts sibling node immediately preceding the match Adding alerts, prefixes, or primary badges inside Appends child element at the end of the matched container Adding fields into groups, pages, or headers attributes Alters attributes on the matched tag in-place Setting invisible, readonly, required, or CSS classes replace Overwrites the matched element and children Discouraged (breaks dependent child modules)

!!! danger "Never Remove Nodes via replace" Avoid using position="replace" to delete fields. If a third-party or downstream OCA module relies on that field or attempts to inherit from it, Odoo will raise an unresolvable XML view error. Prefer hiding elements via position="attributes" with invisible="1".

docs.title: 2. Safely Inheriting Form Views
docs.text:
Form views host business records. This snippet illustrates common mutations: adding conditional fields, modifying attributes with modern domain syntax, and inserting actions in the status bar.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_order_form_inherit_cookbook" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">sale.order.form.inherit.cookbook</field>
        <field name="model">sale.order</field>
        <field name="inherit_id" ref="sale.view_order_form"/>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">

            <!-- 1. Add action button to header bar -->
            <xpath expr="//header" position="inside">
                <button name="action_open_audit_wizard"
                        string="Launch Audit"
                        type="object"
                        class="btn-secondary"
                        invisible="state not in ['draft', 'sent']"/>
            </xpath>

            <!-- 2. Insert field after a target field -->
            <xpath expr="//field[@name='payment_term_id']" position="after">
                <field name="total_weight" readonly="state == 'cancel'"/>
            </xpath>

            <!-- 3. Make an existing field conditionally invisible (Modern Odoo syntax) -->
            <xpath expr="//field[@name='validity_date']" position="attributes">
                <attribute name="invisible">state in ['done', 'cancel']</attribute>
            </xpath>

            <!-- 4. Add a custom notebook tab -->
            <xpath expr="//notebook" position="inside">
                <page string="Technical Specs" name="tech_specs">
                    <group>
                        <group string="Weights">
                            <field name="total_weight"/>
                        </group>
                    </group>
                </page>
            </xpath>

        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: 3. Extending List / Tree Views with Conditional Decorations
docs.text:
List views display tabular collections. Use decoration-* classes (muted, danger, success, warning, info, bf for bold) to highlight rows or columns based on dynamic conditions.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_order_tree_inherit_cookbook" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">sale.order.list.inherit.cookbook</field>
        <field name="model">sale.order</field>
        <field name="inherit_id" ref="sale.view_quotation_tree_with_onboarding"/>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">

            <!-- Apply conditional color styling to the full row -->
            <xpath expr="//list" position="attributes">
                <attribute name="decoration-danger">state == 'cancel'</attribute>
                <attribute name="decoration-success">state == 'sale'</attribute>
            </xpath>

            <!-- Add custom field with optional toggle (can be enabled by user in column selector) -->
            <xpath expr="//field[@name='amount_total']" position="before">
                <field name="total_weight" optional="show" sum="Total Weight"/>
            </xpath>

        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: 4. Extending Search Views (Filters & Group By)
docs.text:
Search views control search bar completions, predefined filters, and group-by clauses.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_sales_order_filter_inherit_cookbook" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">sale.order.search.inherit.cookbook</field>
        <field name="model">sale.order</field>
        <field name="inherit_id" ref="sale.view_sales_order_filter"/>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">

            <!-- 1. Add quick preset filter -->
            <xpath expr="//filter[@name='my_sale_orders_filter']" position="after">
                <filter string="Heavy Shipments (> 50kg)"
                        name="heavy_orders"
                        domain="[('total_weight', '>', 50)]"/>
                <separator/>
            </xpath>

            <!-- 2. Add Group By dimension -->
            <xpath expr="//group" position="inside">
                <filter string="Delivery Date" 
                        name="group_delivery_date" 
                        context="{'group_by': 'commitment_date:month'}"/>
            </xpath>

        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: 5. Kanban View Snippet
docs.text:
Kanban views render card-based visual boards. This snippet illustrates card structure, color pickers, and user avatars.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_custom_task_kanban" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">custom.task.kanban</field>
        <field name="model">custom.task</field>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">
            <kanban default_group_by="state" sample="1">
                <field name="id"/>
                <field name="name"/>
                <field name="user_id"/>
                <field name="state"/>
                <templates>
                    <t t-name="card">
                        <div class="d-flex flex-column">
                            <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-1">
                                <strong class="fs-6"><field name="name"/></strong>
                            </div>
                            <div class="text-muted small">
                                <field name="user_id" widget="many2one_avatar_user"/>
                            </div>
                            <div class="mt-2 d-flex justify-content-end">
                                <field name="state" widget="label_selection"
                                       options="{'classes': {'draft': 'default', 'done': 'success'}}"/>
                            </div>
                        </div>
                    </t>
                </templates>
            </kanban>
        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: 6. Triggering a Wizard Action via XML Button
docs.text:
To invoke a popup wizard directly from a view, trigger an ir.actions.act_window record and pass the source record ID in the context:

<!-- Button in parent form view -->
<button name="%(action_open_mass_update_wizard)d"
        type="action"
        string="Mass Update"
        class="oe_highlight"
        context="{'default_target_model': active_model}"/>

<!-- Window action definition -->
<record id="action_open_mass_update_wizard" model="ir.actions.act_window">
    <field name="name">Status Mass Update</field>
    <field name="res_model">mass.update.wizard</field>
    <field name="view_mode">form</field>
    <field name="target">new</field> <!-- 'new' opens modal popup dialog -->
    <field name="binding_model_id" ref="sale.model_sale_order"/>
    <field name="binding_view_types">list</field> <!-- Appears in Action dropdown in list view -->
</record>

docs.title: Chatter & Mail
docs.text: The OpenERP/Odoo communication engine relies heavily on the mail.thread and mail.activity.mixin mixins. Integrating Chatter into custom business objects provides an audit trail, follower notifications, scheduled activities, and direct messaging out of the box.

docs.title: Core Prerequisites
docs.text: To leverage Chatter features on a custom model, ensure both the model definition and view definitions declare the proper dependencies:

docs.title: 1. Model Mixins
docs.text:
Your model must inherit from mail.thread (for messages/notes) and optionally mail.activity.mixin (for scheduled tasks):

from odoo import models, fields

class CustomProject(models.Model):
    _name = 'custom.project'
    _description = 'Custom Project'
    _inherit = ['mail.thread', 'mail.activity.mixin']

    name = fields.Char(string="Title", required=True, tracking=True)
    state = fields.Selection([
        ('draft', 'Draft'),
        ('in_progress', 'In Progress'),
        ('done', 'Done'),
    ], default='draft', tracking=True)

!!! tip "Field Tracking" Adding tracking=True to fields automatically records all value changes inside the Chatter feed without writing custom Python hooks.

docs.title: 2. View Definition
docs.text:
Append the Chatter widget below the <sheet> tag in your form view:

<sheet>
    <!-- Your form content -->
</sheet>
<chatter/>

docs.title: Message Posting Mechanics
docs.text:
The message_post() method handles all programmatic communication in Odoo. Key subtypes dictate audience visibility:

Subtype XMLID Visual Style Intended Audience Notifications Sent? mail.mt_note Light grey / yellow tint Internal users only No (silent log) mail.mt_comment Standard bubble Record followers & partners Yes (dispatches email)

docs.title: Logging a Note and Sending an Email via Python
docs.text:
This snippet demonstrates silent internal auditing alongside targeted transactional email delivery bypassing background queues:

from odoo import models

class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'

    def action_custom_notification(self):
        for record in self:
            # 1. Post a silent internal note to record history without alerting followers
            record.message_post(
                body="Automated order verification completed successfully.",
                message_type='comment',
                subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note'
            )

            # 2. Dispatch an email using a pre-configured template (immediate delivery)
            template = self.env.ref('sale.email_template_edi_sale', raise_if_not_found=False)
            if template:
                template.send_mail(
                    record.id,
                    force_send=True,
                    email_values={'email_to': 'audit@example.com'}
                )

    def action_post_message_with_attachment(self, file_content_base64, filename):
        """Attaches dynamic binary data directly into the chatter timeline."""
        for record in self:
            record.message_post(
                body="System report generated and attached.",
                subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note',
                attachments=[(filename, file_content_base64)]
            )

docs.title: Wizards (Transient Models)
docs.text: Wizards in Odoo handle interactive, multi-step, or confirmation workflows. They are powered by models.TransientModel, meaning their records are temporary and automatically pruned from the database by an internal vacuum cron job.

docs.title: 1. Core Architecture of a Wizard
docs.text: A complete wizard requires three elements: 1. A Python model inheriting from models.TransientModel. 2. A dedicated Form view with a <footer/> container containing action and cancellation buttons. 3. An action record (ir.actions.act_window) configured with target="new".

docs.title: Python Model (models/sale_order_cancel_wizard.py)
docs.text:
from odoo import models, fields, api
from odoo.exceptions import UserError

class SaleOrderCancelWizard(models.TransientModel):
    _name = 'sale.order.cancel.wizard'
    _description = 'Sale Order Cancellation Wizard'

    order_id = fields.Many2one(
        'sale.order',
        string="Order",
        required=True,
        default=lambda self: self.env.context.get('active_id')
    )
    reason = fields.Selection([
        ('out_of_stock', 'Product Out of Stock'),
        ('customer_request', 'Customer Requested Cancellation'),
        ('price_issue', 'Pricing Discrepancy'),
        ('other', 'Other Reason'),
    ], string="Reason", required=True, default='customer_request')

    additional_notes = fields.Text(string="Additional Notes")

    def action_confirm_cancellation(self):
        """Executes the cancellation workflow and logs context into the chatter."""
        self.ensure_one()
        if not self.order_id:
            raise UserError("No linked order found in context.")

        # Post cancellation reason in order chatter
        note_body = (
            f"<b>Order Cancelled via Wizard</b><br/>"
            f"Reason: {dict(self._fields['reason'].selection).get(self.reason)}<br/>"
            f"Notes: {self.additional_notes or 'N/A'}"
        )
        self.order_id.message_post(body=note_body, subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note')

        # Execute order cancellation
        self.order_id.action_cancel()

        # Close the modal dialog
        return {'type': 'ir.actions.act_window_close'}

docs.title: XML Form View & Action (views/sale_order_cancel_wizard_views.xml)
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="view_sale_order_cancel_wizard_form" model="ir.ui.view">
        <field name="name">sale.order.cancel.wizard.form</field>
        <field name="model">sale.order.cancel.wizard</field>
        <field name="arch" type="xml">
            <form string="Cancel Order">
                <sheet>
                    <group>
                        <field name="order_id" readonly="1"/>
                        <field name="reason"/>
                        <field name="additional_notes" 
                               invisible="reason != 'other'" 
                               required="reason == 'other'"/>
                    </group>
                </sheet>
                <footer>
                    <button name="action_confirm_cancellation" 
                            string="Confirm Cancel" 
                            type="object" 
                            class="btn-danger"/>
                    <button string="Discard" 
                            class="btn-secondary" 
                            special="cancel"/>
                </footer>
            </form>
        </field>
    </record>

    <!-- Action that triggers the modal popup -->
    <record id="action_sale_order_cancel_wizard" model="ir.actions.act_window">
        <field name="name">Cancel Order Confirmation</field>
        <field name="res_model">sale.order.cancel.wizard</field>
        <field name="view_mode">form</field>
        <field name="target">new</field> <!-- Mandatory: renders modal popup -->
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: 2. Multi-Step Wizard (Step-by-Step Flow)
docs.text:
You can build sequential wizards (e.g., Step 1: Options -> Step 2: Confirmation) by managing a state field on the transient record and returning an action reloading the same wizard ID.

from odoo import models, fields

class MultiStepExportWizard(models.TransientModel):
    _name = 'multi.step.export.wizard'
    _description = 'Multi-Step Export Wizard'

    state = fields.Selection([
        ('step1', 'Step 1: Configuration'),
        ('step2', 'Step 2: Summary & Run'),
    ], default='step1')

    export_format = fields.Selection([
        ('csv', 'CSV File'),
        ('xlsx', 'Excel Sheet'),
    ], string="File Format", default='xlsx')

    include_archived = fields.Boolean(string="Include Archived Records")

    def action_go_to_step2(self):
        self.ensure_one()
        self.state = 'step2'
        # Reopen current wizard dialog preserving in-memory state
        return {
            'type': 'ir.actions.act_window',
            'res_model': self._name,
            'res_id': self.id,
            'view_mode': 'form',
            'target': 'new',
        }

    def action_go_to_step1(self):
        self.ensure_one()
        self.state = 'step1'
        return {
            'type': 'ir.actions.act_window',
            'res_model': self._name,
            'res_id': self.id,
            'view_mode': 'form',
            'target': 'new',
        }

    def action_execute(self):
        self.ensure_one()
        # Launch actual business routine here
        return {'type': 'ir.actions.act_window_close'}

Corresponding XML buttons in <footer>: 

<footer>
    <!-- Step 1 Controls -->
    <button name="action_go_to_step2" string="Next" type="object" class="btn-primary" invisible="state != 'step1'"/>

    <!-- Step 2 Controls -->
    <button name="action_go_to_step1" string="Back" type="object" class="btn-secondary" invisible="state != 'step2'"/>
    <button name="action_execute" string="Start Processing" type="object" class="btn-primary" invisible="state != 'step2'"/>

    <button string="Cancel" class="btn-secondary" special="cancel"/>
</footer>

docs.title: Actions & Scheduled Tasks (Cron)
docs.text: This page covers automated processing, asynchronous scheduled cron tasks (ir.cron), and contextual Server Actions (ir.actions.server) in Odoo 17 and 18.

docs.title: 1. Scheduled Actions (ir.cron)
docs.text: Cron jobs run tasks automatically in the background at designated time intervals.

docs.title: Python Model Handler (models/sale_order_automation.py)
docs.text:
Always structure cron methods as batch handlers with defensive error handling so a single failing record does not abort the entire scheduled job:

import logging
from datetime import timedelta
from odoo import models, fields, api

_logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'

    @api.model
    def _cron_auto_expire_quotations(self):
        """Scans for overdue quotations and transitions them to 'cancel'."""
        cutoff_date = fields.Date.today() - timedelta(days=30)
        expired_quotes = self.search([
            ('state', 'in', ['draft', 'sent']),
            ('create_date', '<', cutoff_date)
        ])

        _logger.info("Auto-expiring %d quotations older than %s", len(expired_quotes), cutoff_date)

        for quote in expired_quotes:
            try:
                quote.action_cancel()
                quote.message_post(
                    body="Quotation automatically cancelled due to 30 days of inactivity.",
                    subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note'
                )
            except Exception as e:
                _logger.error("Failed to auto-expire quotation ID %s: %s", quote.id, str(e))

docs.title: Cron XML Definition (data/cron_data.xml)
docs.text:
Register the cron in an XML file included under data in __manifest__.py:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <data noupdate="1">
        <record id="ir_cron_auto_expire_quotations" model="ir.cron">
            <field name="name">Sale Order: Auto Expire Inactive Quotations</field>
            <field name="model_id" ref="sale.model_sale_order"/>
            <field name="state">code</field>
            <field name="code">model._cron_auto_expire_quotations()</field>
            <field name="interval_number">1</field>
            <field name="interval_type">days</field>
            <field name="numbercall">-1</field> <!-- -1 indicates indefinite repetitions -->
            <field name="active">True</field>
            <field name="nextcall" eval="(DateTime.now() + relativedelta(days=1)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d 02:00:00')"/>
            <field name="priority">5</field>
        </record>
    </data>
</odoo>

!!! warning "noupdate='1'" Always wrap cron definitions inside <data noupdate="1">. This prevents module updates from overriding custom execution times, toggled active statuses, or interval adjustments made by database administrators in production.

docs.title: 2. Server Actions (ir.actions.server)
docs.text: Server actions allow running Python code from UI buttons, contextual Action menus (batch actions), or automated triggers.

docs.title: Adding a Batch Action to the UI "Actions" Gear
docs.text:
This definition binds a server action directly to the Actions menu on list and form views for sale.order:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="action_mark_orders_as_reviewed" model="ir.actions.server">
        <field name="name">Mark as Reviewed</field>
        <field name="model_id" ref="sale.model_sale_order"/>
        <field name="binding_model_id" ref="sale.model_sale_order"/>
        <field name="binding_view_types">list,form</field>
        <field name="state">code</field>
        <field name="code">
# 'records' represents the recordset selected in the view
for record in records:
    if record.state == 'draft':
        record.message_post(body="Batch reviewed by manager.")
        </field>
    </record>
</odoo>

docs.title: Contextual Variables in Server Action Code
docs.text:
When writing Python code inside <field name="code">, the execution context provides several built-in variables:

Variable Description env The current Odoo Environment instance model The ir.model object corresponding to the action record Active single record (in form view) records Recordset of selected items (in list view) action Action dictionary returned to the web client (optional) time, datetime, dateutil Standard date/time modules available out of the box

docs.title: 3. Triggering Client Action / Window Action from Python
docs.text:
Return an action dictionary directly from your Python methods to redirect users or display notifications:

def action_view_related_invoices(self):
    self.ensure_one()
    return {
        'name': 'Customer Invoices',
        'type': 'ir.actions.act_window',
        'res_model': 'account.move',
        'view_mode': 'list,form', # In Odoo 18 use 'list,form' (tree is legacy)
        'domain': [('partner_id', '=', self.partner_id.id), ('move_type', '=', 'out_invoice')],
        'context': {'default_partner_id': self.partner_id.id},
    }

docs.title: OWL & Frontend JavaScript
docs.text:
Odoo 18.0 Odoo 19.0 Odoo 20.0 Ready

Odoo's frontend is entirely powered by the Odoo Web Library (OWL). Starting from Odoo 16, and solidifying through Odoo 18, 19, and 20, legacy widgets have been entirely replaced by OWL components, hooks, and registries.

docs.title: 1. Creating a Custom Field Component
docs.text:
To create a new field type (e.g., a custom text input that converts text to uppercase), you need a JavaScript component and to register it in the fields registry.

/** @odoo-module **/

import { Component, xml } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { standardFieldProps } from "@web/views/fields/standard_field_props";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

export class UppercaseCharField extends Component {
    static template = xml`
        <div class="o_uppercase_field">
            <input 
                type="text" 
                class="o_input"
                t-att-value="props.record.data[props.name]"
                t-on-change="onChange"
            />
        </div>
    `;

    static props = {
        ...standardFieldProps,
    };

    setup() {
        this.notificationService = useService("notification");
    }

    onChange(ev) {
        const newValue = ev.target.value.toUpperCase();

        // Update the record's value in the model
        this.props.record.update({ [this.props.name]: newValue });

        // Use a standard service (notification)
        this.notificationService.add("Value converted to uppercase", {
            type: "success",
        });
    }
}

// Register the component so it can be used in XML views as widget="uppercase_char"
registry.category("fields").add("uppercase_char", {
    component: UppercaseCharField,
});

To use this in your XML form view: 

<field name="my_char_field" widget="uppercase_char"/>

docs.title: 2. Patching an Existing Component
docs.text:
Often, you want to extend an existing component (like the FormController or a standard widget) to add a lifecycle hook or intercept a method. In modern Odoo, we use the patch utility.

/** @odoo-module **/

import { FormController } from "@web/views/form/form_controller";
import { patch } from "@web/core/utils/patch";
import { onWillStart } from "@odoo/owl";

patch(FormController.prototype, {

    setup() {
        super.setup(...arguments);

        onWillStart(async () => {
            console.log("Form view is about to start loading...");
        });
    },

    async saveButtonClicked() {
        // Intercept the save action
        console.log("Intercepted save button click!");

        // Always call the super method to maintain standard behavior
        return await super.saveButtonClicked(...arguments);
    }
});

!!! tip "Patching best practices" Always call super.methodName(...arguments) when overriding existing functions to avoid breaking the core framework logic. Do not use arrow functions if you need access to this via super.

docs.title: 3. Utilizing Standard Services (RPC, ORM, Notification)
docs.text:
Odoo provides several services that can be injected into any OWL component using the useService hook.

/** @odoo-module **/

import { Component } from "@odoo/owl";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

export class MyCustomAction extends Component {
    setup() {
        this.rpc = useService("rpc");
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.actionService = useService("action");
    }

    async fetchCustomData() {
        // Option 1: Direct JSON-RPC call to a controller route
        const result = await this.rpc("/my_module/custom_route", {
            param1: "value",
        });

        // Option 2: ORM call (search_read, call, etc.) directly to a model
        const records = await this.orm.searchRead("res.partner", [['is_company', '=', true]], ["name", "email"]);

        // Option 3: Trigger a window action
        this.actionService.doAction({
            type: 'ir.actions.act_window',
            res_model: 'res.partner',
            view_mode: 'list,form',
            views: [[false, 'list'], [false, 'form']],
        });
    }
}

docs.title: Migration & Version Guide (17 to 20)
docs.text:
Odoo 18.0 Odoo 19.0 Odoo 20.0 Ready

Odoo's framework evolves rapidly. Between Odoo 17 and Odoo 20, several major structural changes were finalized. This guide highlights the key syntactical shifts you must implement to ensure your modules remain compatible with modern Odoo versions.

docs.title: 1. The Death of <tree> (Replaced by <list>)
docs.text:
In earlier versions, tabular views were defined using the <tree> tag. Starting heavily in Odoo 17, standardizing in 18, and strictly enforced in 19 and 20, the tag is now officially <list>.

Legacy Syntax (Pre-17): 

<record id="view_partner_tree" model="ir.ui.view">
    <field name="arch" type="xml">
        <tree string="Partners">
            <field name="name"/>
        </tree>
    </field>
</record>

Modern Syntax (18, 19, 20): 

<record id="view_partner_list" model="ir.ui.view">
    <!-- Notice the view_mode is 'list', not 'tree' -->
    <field name="arch" type="xml">
        <list string="Partners">
            <field name="name"/>
        </list>
    </field>
</record>
Note: In your window actions (ir.actions.act_window), ensure view_mode specifies list,form instead of tree,form.

docs.title: 2. Deprecation of the attrs Dictionary
docs.text:
Previously, conditional modifiers (invisible, readonly, required) were packed into a Python-like dictionary evaluated by the client. This is completely deprecated.

Legacy Syntax (Pre-17): 

<field name="vat" attrs="{'invisible': [('is_company', '=', False)], 'readonly': [('state', '=', 'done')]}"/>

Modern Syntax (18, 19, 20): Attributes are now directly placed on the tag, containing standard Python domain expressions.

<field name="vat" 
       invisible="not is_company" 
       readonly="state == 'done'"/>

docs.title: 3. Manifest Versioning Standard
docs.text:
To adhere to OCA (Odoo Community Association) standards, always format the version key in your __manifest__.py combining the targeted Odoo version and your module's semantic version.

  • For Odoo 18: 'version': '18.0.1.0.0'
  • For Odoo 19: 'version': '19.0.1.0.0'
  • For Odoo 20: 'version': '20.0.1.0.0'
{
    'name': 'My Custom Module',
    'version': '20.0.1.0.0',
    'depends': ['base', 'web'],
    'data': [
        'security/ir.model.access.csv',
        'views/my_model_views.xml',
    ],
    'assets': {
        'web.assets_backend': [
            'my_custom_module/static/src/**/*',
        ],
    },
}

docs.title: 4. Assets Declaration
docs.text:
The way JavaScript, CSS, and SCSS assets are loaded shifted significantly in Odoo 15+ and remains standard through 20. Never use <template id="assets_backend" inherit_id="web.assets_backend"> inside XML files anymore.

All assets must be declared inside the __manifest__.py under the 'assets' dictionary using glob patterns (**/* is fully supported).

docs.title: Best Practices & Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
Odoo 18.0 Odoo 19.0 Odoo 20.0 Ready

Developing in Odoo can sometimes be tricky. Below is a collection of the most common pitfalls, hidden traps, and architectural best practices to keep your code fast, safe, and bug-free.

docs.title: 1. The "Expected Singleton" Error
docs.text:
This is the most common Odoo error. It happens when you try to access a field or call a method on a recordset containing multiple records, but the code expects only one.

Wrong Way: 

def action_do_something(self):
    # If 'self' contains 3 records, this crashes with ValueError: Expected singleton
    if self.state == 'draft':
        self.state = 'done'

Correct Way (Looping or ensure_one): 

def action_do_something(self):
    # Option A: Handle multiple records gracefully
    for record in self:
        if record.state == 'draft':
            record.state = 'done'

def action_print_report(self):
    # Option B: Force a singleton (crashes early if multiple records are passed)
    self.ensure_one() 
    return self.env.ref('my_module.my_report_action').report_action(self)

docs.title: 2. The N+1 Query Problem (Performance)
docs.text:
Writing or searching inside a for loop generates massive amounts of SQL queries, slowing down the system significantly. Always use batch operations.

Wrong Way (Very Slow): 

for order in self:
    # Executes a SQL query for EVERY single order in the loop
    lines = self.env['sale.order.line'].search([('order_id', '=', order.id)])
    order.write({'is_processed': True}) # Executes an UPDATE query per order

Correct Way (Fast & Optimized): 

# One single SQL query to fetch all lines for all orders
all_lines = self.env['sale.order.line'].search([('order_id', 'in', self.ids)])

# One single SQL query to update all orders at once
self.write({'is_processed': True})

docs.title: 3. Elevating Privileges and Multi-Company Context
docs.text:
Sometimes a user needs to trigger an action (like confirming an order) that creates records in another model where they don't have write access, or in a specific company environment.

def action_advanced_process(self):
    for record in self:
        # 1. sudo() bypasses record rules and access rights (use with caution)
        # 2. with_company() ensures accounting entries are created in the correct company
        record.env['account.move'].sudo().with_company(record.company_id).create({
            'move_type': 'out_invoice',
            'partner_id': record.partner_id.id,
            'company_id': record.company_id.id,
        })

docs.title: 4. Preventing Deletion of Processed Records
docs.text:
By default, users with delete access can remove records anytime. It is a best practice to override the unlink method to prevent deleting records that are already confirmed.

from odoo.exceptions import UserError

class SaleOrder(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'sale.order'

    def unlink(self):
        for record in self:
            if record.state not in ['draft', 'cancel']:
                raise UserError("You can only delete draft or cancelled orders.")
        # Call super to perform the actual deletion
        return super().unlink()

docs.title: 5. The "NewId" Trap in Computes and Onchanges
docs.text:
When Odoo processes @api.depends or @api.onchange on a form before it is saved, the record doesn't exist in the database yet. Its ID is a virtual NewId. If you try to pass this ID to an external API, a raw SQL query, or another environment, it will crash.

Problem (Crashes on unsaved records): 

@api.depends('amount')
def _compute_external_sync(self):
    for record in self:
        # If 'record' is not saved yet, record.id is an object like <NewId 0x...>
        self.env.cr.execute("SELECT * FROM some_table WHERE order_id = %s", [record.id])

Correct Way (Using _origin): 

@api.depends('amount')
def _compute_external_sync(self):
    for record in self:
        # _origin returns the actual database record (if it exists) or an empty recordset
        real_id = record._origin.id
        if real_id:
            self.env.cr.execute("SELECT * FROM some_table WHERE order_id = %s", [real_id])

docs.title: 6. Broken Transactions (Savepoints)
docs.text:
If you try to catch an exception (e.g., a constraint violation or a database lock) using a try/except block, Odoo's database cursor will still be marked as "failed". Any subsequent ORM operation in the same transaction will crash with a psycopg2 InternalError.

Wrong Way (Transaction gets poisoned): 

def action_sync_all(self):
    for record in self:
        try:
            record.action_risky_sync() # If this raises a DB error...
        except Exception:
            # ...the cursor is broken. The next loop iteration will crash immediately!
            continue

Correct Way (Using Savepoints): 

def action_sync_all(self):
    for record in self:
        try:
            # Create a savepoint before the risky operation
            with self.env.cr.savepoint():
                record.action_risky_sync()
        except Exception as e:
            # If it fails, only this specific savepoint is rolled back.
            # The transaction stays healthy for the next records.
            record.message_post(body=f"Sync failed: {e}")

docs.title: 7. Context Pollution (Default values leaking)
docs.text:
When you pass the context to a new window action or a method, it often contains keys like default_name or default_partner_id. If you use this context to create other unrelated records (e.g., logging a history line), Odoo will try to apply those default_* keys to the new model, often causing crashes if the fields don't exist.

Wrong Way: 

def create_invoice(self):
    # If self.env.context contains 'default_type': 'sale', it leaks into the wizard!
    return self.env['some.wizard'].create({
        'order_id': self.id
    })

Correct Way (Clean the context): 

def create_invoice(self):
    # Remove specific dangerous keys, or pass a completely clean context
    clean_context = dict(self.env.context)
    clean_context.pop('default_type', None)

    return self.env['some.wizard'].with_context(clean_context).create({
        'order_id': self.id
    })

docs.title: 8. Raw SQL Bypasses the ORM Cache
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to use self.env.cr.execute() for massive performance gains. However, raw SQL entirely bypasses the Odoo ORM. This means the ORM cache is not updated, and computed fields depending on your changes will not trigger.

Wrong Way (Cache is out of sync): 

def action_mass_update(self):
    # Updates the database directly
    self.env.cr.execute("UPDATE sale_order SET state = 'done' WHERE id IN %s", [tuple(self.ids)])

    for order in self:
        # WRONG: The ORM cache still thinks the state is whatever it was before the SQL query!
        print(order.state)

Correct Way (Invalidate the cache): 

def action_mass_update(self):
    self.env.cr.execute("UPDATE sale_order SET state = 'done' WHERE id IN %s", [tuple(self.ids)])

    # Clear the cache for these specific records so the ORM fetches fresh data
    self.invalidate_recordset(['state']) 

    # Or, if you updated multiple tables: self.env.invalidate_all()

docs.title: 9. The Timezone Illusion (UTC vs Local Time)
docs.text:
In Odoo, fields.Datetime is always stored in UTC in the PostgreSQL database. It is only converted to the user's local timezone visually in the frontend. If you do date math in Python or format a datetime to a string without converting it first, your times will be off by several hours.

Wrong Way (Printing raw UTC): 

def print_time(self):
    # If the user is in Rome (UTC+2) and creates a record at 14:00, 
    # the DB stores 12:00. This will print 12:00!
    return f"Created at: {self.create_date.strftime('%H:%M')}"

Correct Way (Converting to user's timezone): 

import pytz
from odoo.tools import format_datetime

def print_time(self):
    # Option A: Use Odoo's built-in formatting tool (handles tz and lang automatically)
    local_time_str = format_datetime(self.env, self.create_date, dt_format='HH:mm')

    # Option B: Manual timezone conversion using pytz
    user_tz = pytz.timezone(self.env.user.tz or 'UTC')
    local_dt = self.create_date.replace(tzinfo=pytz.utc).astimezone(user_tz)

docs.title: 10. Modifying One2many/Many2many with Command
docs.text:
In older Odoo versions, you had to use weird tuple structures like (0, 0, {}) or (4, id) to modify relation fields. Since Odoo 16+, and heavily enforced in Odoo 18-20, you should use the Command namespace. It prevents syntax errors and makes your code self-documenting.

Wrong Way (Old Tuple Syntax): 

def add_lines(self):
    self.write({
        'line_ids': [
            (0, 0, {'product_id': 1, 'price': 10}), # Create
            (4, 5, False),                          # Link existing ID 5
            (5, 0, 0)                               # Unlink all
        ]
    })

Correct Way (Modern Command Class): 

from odoo import Command

def add_lines(self):
    self.write({
        'line_ids': [
            Command.create({'product_id': 1, 'price': 10}),
            Command.link(5),
            Command.clear()
        ]
    })
